planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; twister haworthia tolerates lower light than sun-loving succulents and scorches in direct hot sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; twister haworthia tolerates lower light than sun-loving succulents and scorches in direct hot sun. Narrow, dark green leaves are held in a dense, irregularly twisted, four-ranked spiral that gives the rosette a restless, propeller-like look quite different from the flat or tightly coiled rosettes of other Haworthiopsis species. Native to the Western Cape of South Africa, it stays compact and slow-growing, making it well suited to a shallow succulent dish or crowded windowsill collection. Water only once the soil has dried completely, keep it out of hot direct sun, and separate basal offsets to propagate new plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in a shaded container with overhead cover from winter rain in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; pad haworthia is only reliably grown under glass or roof protection, not as an outdoor garden plant.

directions: Grow in a shaded container with overhead cover from winter rain in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; pad haworthia is only reliably grown under glass or roof protection, not as an outdoor garden plant. Thick, firm, paddle-shaped leaves are arranged in a low, rounded rosette with a dull, grayish-green surface roughened by fine raised tubercles, a subdued texture distinct from the glossier or more sharply banded leaves of related species. Native to a narrow area of South Africa's Little Karoo, it rarely offsets and grows very slowly, so it is usually propagated from seed rather than division. Water sparingly, letting the gritty mix dry fully between waterings, and protect it from prolonged summer humidity and rain, which it does not tolerate well in cultivation.

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring as new growth begins; this is the wild species behind the popular 'Freddie' cultivar and shares its narrow, striped leaves.

directions: Goeppertia concinna is the wild species behind the compact 'Freddie' cultivar, producing the same narrow, lance-shaped leaves marked with paired dark green stripes radiating out from the midrib like a leopard's spots, though the species itself can grow slightly larger and looser than its popular cultivar. It prefers bright indirect to shaded light, consistently moist soil, and high humidity, since dry air and mineral-laden tap water both cause brown, crispy leaf margins. Keep it out of direct sun, which bleaches the contrasting striped pattern, and divide crowded rhizome clumps in spring to propagate and refresh the planting.

common_name: Majestic Prayer Plant (White Star Calathea Species)

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring as new growth begins; this upright species is the parent of the striped 'Whitestar' cultivar and needs steady warmth and humidity.

directions: Native to lowland forests of northern South America, Goeppertia majestica grows tall, upright, oblong leaves on long petioles, with the wild form showing fine pale feathered striping over deep green above and a rich maroon-purple underside, a bolder and more vertical habit than smaller mat-forming calatheas. It is the parent species behind the 'Whitestar' cultivar and shares its need for bright indirect light, evenly moist humus-rich soil, and humidity well above 50 percent to prevent curling or browning leaf edges. Keep it away from cold drafts and direct sun, feed lightly during the growing season, and divide rhizome clumps in spring to propagate.

planting.note: Grow as a hanging-basket houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; cupid peperomia trails readily and roots easily from stem cuttings.

directions: Grow as a hanging-basket houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; cupid peperomia trails readily and roots easily from stem cuttings. Native to understory forests from Brazil to northern Argentina, it produces slender, trailing stems lined with small, glossy, heart-shaped leaves, a looser and more cascading habit than the upright or rosette-forming peperomias common in cultivation. Let the top inch or two of potting mix dry before watering again, and avoid letting the pot sit in standing water, since the thin trailing stems are prone to rot if kept too wet. Pinch trailing stems to encourage fuller branching and propagate new plants easily from stem-tip cuttings rooted in water or moist soil.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky succulent mix; pleated peperomia stores water in its folded leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky succulent mix; pleated peperomia stores water in its folded leaves and prefers to dry out between waterings. Thick, semi-succulent leaves fold lengthwise along a central crease like a closed book, giving the foliage a distinctive pleated, ribbed texture unlike the flat or quilted leaves of most other peperomias. It tolerates lower light than true desert succulents, making it a reasonable windowsill companion for haworthias and gasterias, but still needs the soil to dry fully between waterings to avoid stem rot. Water from the base and let excess drain away completely, and propagate easily from leaf or stem cuttings allowed to callus briefly before potting.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Grow as a terrarium or hanging houseplant in bright, indirect light with consistent moisture and high humidity; red trailing peperomia dislikes soggy soil as much as prolonged drought.

directions: Grow as a terrarium or hanging houseplant in bright, indirect light with consistent moisture and high humidity; red trailing peperomia dislikes soggy soil as much as prolonged drought. Small, fleshy, elliptical leaves grow in whorled clusters of four along wiry, distinctly red stems, with the leaf undersides also flushed red, giving the whole plant a warm reddish cast that stands out against greener peperomias. Keep the soil evenly moist but fast-draining, mist regularly or grow under a terrarium lid to maintain humidity, and avoid cold drafts, which cause the delicate stems to collapse. Propagate by rooting short stem-tip cuttings in moist, airy potting mix.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in partial shade to shade in airy, fast-draining, peat- or coir-based potting mix; parallel peperomia is one of the more shade-tolerant peperomias and can be allowed to dry between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in partial shade to shade in airy, fast-draining, peat- or coir-based potting mix; parallel peperomia is one of the more shade-tolerant peperomias and can be allowed to dry between waterings. Native to South American forest understories, it produces compact, semi-succulent leaves marked with fine parallel veining in alternating light and dark green bands, a subtler striped texture than the bolder watermelon-patterned peperomias. Let the top few inches of mix dry out before watering again, since its semi-succulent leaves and stems store enough moisture to tolerate missed waterings far better than overly wet soil. Propagate from leaf or stem cuttings rooted in a light, airy mix blended with perlite and orchid bark.
